newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-S.Electric promises offset profit dip.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-S.Electric promises offset profit dip.

text.p: Britain's last independent regional electricity company (Rec) Southern Electric Plc reported lower year-end profits as expected on Wednesday and hinted at cost cuts and future benefits to shareholders.
Pretax profits for the year ending March 31 were 255.5 million pounds ($417.1 million) compared with 283 million a year ago, as Southern felt the impact of regulatory price reviews.
The market shrugged off the profit dip and focused on Southern's promises. Its shares were up 3.5 pence at 402 pence by 1400 GMT, off a day's high of 405 pence.
"It was a solid set of results. They are certainly kitted up to return value to shareholders and there seems to be more cost cutting to come," said Nigel Hawkins, an analyst at Yamaichi.

"We're committed to using the balance sheet strength to maximise shareholder value," finance director Ian Marchant told Reuters. But he added there were no immediate plans due to uncertainty over a proposed one-off "windfall" tax expected to be announced in a government budget on July 2.
Marchant said that there was "more to go for in reducing costs" in distribution, but declined to set targets.
Southern said it had cut controllable costs by 14.6 percent over the year, making a cumulative reduction of 45 percent in real terms over the last six years.
"That's a phenomenal cost reduction. The numbers look very good against that background," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.

Southern has already spent around 156 million pounds on a share buyback earlier this year after being outbid by Scottish Power in a takeover tussle for Southern Water last year. Analysts said Southern would please the market if it made another return of value.
"The market would be keen on some sort of buyback or special dividend, but not necessarily this year. Southern could see the windfall tax as this year's payout," the analyst said.
Southern, along with other privatised utilities, could be subject to the tax proposed by the new Labour government on excess profits aimed at funding a three billion pound scheme to cut unemployment.
Details including amounts and companies affected are expected in the July 2 budget.
Southern's own plans to merge with generator National Power were frustrated when the previous Conservative government blocked the deal as anti-competitive over a year ago.

Southern, which was left on the shelf after a flurry of takeovers saw the other 11 Recs snapped up, is considered well defended against a takeover because of its two billion pounds or so value and its strong management independence.

But Marchant ruled out pressure on the company to use the strength of its balance sheet to make its own acquisition. Southern was confident that its existing businesses would allow dividend growth of five to eight percent in real terms over the next three years.
Southern said in a statement that it was aiming at growth for its four key businesses -- distribution, supply, generation and contracting.
It should achieve long-term earnings growth through profit contribution from non-regulated earnings and future investment in generation.
Plans for two 45-megaWatt (mW) open-cycle gas-fired power stations were well advanced with a further five sites identified for similar plants.

It will invest around 100 million pounds in these projects over the next few years and Marchant said they should provide "quite significant earnings growth from 2000 and beyond". Southern's maximum demand last year was 5,700 mW, he said.
He added that the company was also looking outside its own area for generation possibilities.
Southern also expected liberalisation of the domestic market, scheduled to start in April 1998, to be an area of opportunity. It was "well placed for growth as a leading national supplier".
Southern would be ready to enter testing of the market in January, he said, and was confident of being ready on time for the opening up of the market from April.
($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
